Regulators Open Inquiry Into Cloud Outage That Knocked Out Half the Internet

By A. Reporter — Updated August 21, 2026

Federal regulators said Friday they had opened a formal inquiry into the outage that took a major cloud provider offline for nearly six hours this week, disrupting banking apps, airline check-in systems and thousands of smaller websites that rely on the platform's infrastructure.

The outage began just after 2 a.m. Eastern time when an automated configuration change propagated to a core routing layer faster than the provider's internal safeguards could halt it, according to a preliminary incident report the company published Thursday night. Engineers said the rollback itself took longer than expected because the same routing layer that failed was also used to coordinate the fix.

By the time service was fully restored, more than nine thousand companies had reported some form of disruption, according to a tally kept by an independent outage-tracking service. Several banks temporarily disabled mobile check deposits, and at least two airlines reverted to manual check-in procedures at a handful of major airports.

In a statement, the agency said its inquiry would focus on whether the concentration of critical infrastructure among a small number of cloud providers now poses a systemic risk comparable to those regulators historically reserved for the banking sector. "When a single misconfiguration can affect emergency services, payment processing and air travel simultaneously, that is no longer just a vendor's customer service problem," the agency's statement read.

The cloud provider said it would publish a full post-incident report within thirty days and had already rolled back the change management process implicated in the outage. Industry analysts said the inquiry was unlikely to produce binding rules quickly, but could shape how regulators approach cloud concentration risk going forward.
